theme: God speaks creation into existence; the six days; the goodness of all things
settingTheScene:
Genesis is the first book of the Pentateuch, the five books of Moses, and was written for Israel as they prepared to enter the land God promised to Abraham. The original audience had just been delivered from slavery in Egypt, where they had lived for four hundred years under a culture full of competing gods: the sun, the river, the storm, and Pharaoh himself, who was called divine. Genesis 1 was a direct answer to all of that. It told them whose world they actually lived in.

This opening chapter is also the beginning of the entire biblical story, the foundation on which every covenant, every promise, and every redemptive act will rest. Before there can be a story of redemption, there must first be a creation worth redeeming. Before there can be a Savior, there must first be a Creator. Genesis 1 tells us who God is, what kind of world he made, and what humanity was made for. Everything that follows in Scripture depends on getting this beginning right.
observation: The chapter follows a clear pattern: “And God said… and it was so… and God saw that it was good.” Notice how often this rhythm repeats. Counting them is itself an act of observation.

There is a parallel structure between the days. Days 1-3 form realms (light/dark, sky/sea, land/vegetation), and Days 4-6 fill those realms with their inhabitants (sun and moon, fish and birds, animals and humans). Creation is ordered, not chaotic.
God speaks. He does not struggle, fight, or shape creation out of pre-existing material that opposes him. He commands, and reality obeys.

The creation of humanity is set apart. There is a divine deliberation (“Let us make man in our image”), a doubling of the verb “created” in verse 27, and the explicit blessing and commission given to no other creature.
The seventh day is the climax, not the sixth. The creation of humanity is the high point of the work, but the Sabbath is the high point of the week.
The phrase “it was good” appears seven times. After humanity is made, it becomes “very good.” Goodness is woven into the fabric of what God has made.
interpretation:
Genesis 1 is not primarily concerned with how God created or how long it took. Its concern is who God is, what he made, and what kind of world we live in. Every other ancient creation story in the world that Israel encountered, Babylonian, Egyptian, Canaanite, featured gods who fought, struggled, killed one another, or formed the world out of corpses and chaos. Genesis 1 stands utterly apart. There is one God. He is sovereign over all things. He creates by speaking, not by struggling. And what he makes is good.

The opening verse establishes everything: “In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.” Before there was time, there was God. Before there was matter, there was God. He is not part of the created order; he is its source. The Hebrew word for “created” here is bara, a verb used only of God, never of human making. It signals something only God can do: bring into existence what was not there before.

Then comes the pattern. God speaks, and what he says becomes reality. Light comes into being at his word. Land separates from sea at his word. Plants grow, stars appear, creatures swim and fly and walk, all at his word. This is the doctrine of creation by divine speech, and it carries enormous theological weight. It means God’s word is not advisory or decorative; it is creative. What God says, is. When you later read that the gospel comes to you “through the word,” or that you are “born again by the imperishable seed of the word,” remember that the same word that called galaxies into existence is now calling sinners into new life.

The chapter unfolds in a deliberate, beautiful symmetry. Days 1, 2, and 3 form realms, God separates light from darkness, waters above from waters below, and dry land from sea. Days 4, 5, and 6 fill those realms, sun and moon for day and night, birds and fish for sky and sea, animals and humans for the land. The world is not random. It is shaped, ordered, and prepared like a home being made ready for its inhabitants. And the chief inhabitant for whom the home is prepared is humanity.

When the sixth day arrives, the pattern shifts. God deliberates: “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness.” The plural is striking, Christian readers have long seen here the first hint of the triune nature of God, though the doctrine of the Trinity is not yet articulated. What is articulated is that humanity is unique. Of every other creature, God said “Let the earth bring forth” or “Let the waters swarm.” But of humanity, God said “Let us make.” Humanity bears God’s image, male and female together, blessed, commissioned, and given responsibility over creation. This is the foundation of all Christian anthropology. Every human you will ever meet bears the image of God.

And then, on the seventh day, God rests. Not because he is tired. He rests because the work is finished, and rest is the goal of the work. The Sabbath is woven into the fabric of creation before any law is given. It tells us that the universe has a purpose, and that purpose is not endless production but communion with God in restful joy. Every Sabbath the church gathers, every Lord’s Day a believer enters worship, points back to this seventh day, and forward to the eternal rest that awaits the people of God.
connection: Day 1 is the foundation. There is no previous reading to build on, but everything that follows in this plan will build on this. The God who speaks here is the same God who will call Abraham, deliver Israel from Egypt, give the law at Sinai, raise up David, send his Son, and pour out his Spirit. The world he makes here is the same world that will be cursed in Genesis 3, redeemed at the cross, and renewed in the new heavens and new earth. Watch how often the rest of Scripture echoes this chapter: John’s Gospel opens “In the beginning was the Word,” directly mirroring Genesis 1:1. Revelation closes with a new creation that fulfills what began here. The whole Bible is in some sense the story of how God brings his good creation to its appointed rest in Christ.
application:
Begin where Scripture begins: with God as Creator. This is not a doctrine you accept once and move past. It is the lens through which you see everything else. Because God made you, you have inherent dignity that no one can give and no one can take. Because God made your body, your body is not a prison or an accident, it is good. Because God made the world, your work in the world matters; gardening, parenting, building, studying, serving are all forms of carrying out the mandate given to humanity in the image of God. Because God made the Sabbath, your rest is not laziness but worship.

Today, consider one practical response: where in your life have you been treating something God made as either worthless or as ultimate? The created order points beyond itself to its Creator. Eat your food with gratitude. Take in a sunset and let it lead you to praise. Treat the people around you as image-bearers worthy of dignity. And when you grow tired, let your weariness remind you that the goal of creation is not endless work but the rest of God himself, a rest finally fulfilled in Christ.
readingInstruction: Read Genesis 1:1-2:3 slowly, and aloud if you can. It is the opening of the Bible and takes about five minutes. Notice the rhythm of the six days and the line that keeps returning: “And God saw that it was good.” Read it once for the story, and once more asking what it tells you about God.
prayerPrompts: Praise God as Creator, and thank him for one thing in your life you have received as a gift from his hand.
Ask him to open your eyes to see his goodness in ordinary things today.
Tell him what you want to learn about him as you begin this journey.
